title: Blessings of the heart
hookLine: respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, and being easy to correct

cards: Someone at work points out a mistake in your report. Not cruelly; it's just wrong. And there's a tiny moment, maybe half a second, before you answer.
A lot rides on that half second. Do you bristle, explain, defend? Or do you say: oh, you're right, thanks?

The Mangala Sutta has a word for the second answer, and it calls it one of the highest blessings. So far the poem has covered company, learning, home and work. Now it reaches the qualities inside a person.

teach.b: The verse goes: respect and humility, contentment and gratitude, and hearing the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing.
Then the next: patience, being easy to correct, seeing those who live a holy life, and talking about the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Look at gratitude.
The Pali is kataññuta. Kata, what was done; ññu, knowing.
Gratitude is knowing what has been done for you. Not a feeling you have to manufacture. A kind of seeing: someone made this meal, someone taught me to read, someone kept the lights on.
The Buddha elsewhere says that grateful people, those who know what has been done for them, are rare in the world.
And look at being easy to correct, sovacassata. Literally, being good to speak to.

teach.h: A WEEK OF WHAT A PERSON DOES
teach.b: The person you can tell something to without a fight. It sits right next to patience, and it's the half-second answer from the report. These are blessings because they open a person.
Contentment leaves room. Humility lets teaching in.
Gratitude lets you see. Look back at the week. The sage with no fear-built ties.
The jewel, chanted on a truth. The smell of deeds, not of food. A friend you can rest on.
Then wise company, home, and now the heart. Again and again this week, the good thing turned out to be something a person does or is, not something that happens to them.

how: Many Buddhists practice gratitude through daily chanting, offerings to monastics and teachers, and merit-dedication ceremonies for parents and ancestors.

o: gratitude: knowing what was done for you
politeness: saying thank you on time
a debt you must pay back in full

games.q: blessings of the heart: tap the pairs.

s: the Pali word for gratitude means knowing what has been done
kata, what was done; ññu, knowing.
being easy to correct is listed among the highest blessings
sovacassata, being good to speak to, sits beside patience.
the poem treats gratitude as a feeling you must force
it's a kind of seeing: knowing what was done for you.

games.q: a coworker points out a real mistake in your work. you have half a second. what does the blessings poem call the good answer?
games.why: sovacassata, being easy to speak to and correct, is one of the highest blessings, listed right beside patience.

practice: Look at one thing near you, a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing, and trace what was done for it to be here: someone grew the cotton, someone sewed, someone drove the truck, someone stocked the shelf.
Don't force a warm feeling; just know what was done, then let one person who did something for you come to mind, and know that too.

wordCard.voice: Kataññuta, gratitude. In the Mangala Sutta: respect, humility, contentment, patience and being easy to correct, the blessings that open a person. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kataññuta: gratitude, literally knowing what has been done (for you).

carryVoice: Your line: gratitude is a blessing. It starts with seeing what was done. That's day five hundred ninety-five.
